justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a broadly stable outlook for the asset, with only modest drift upward over time. At the one-day horizon, I anchored closely to the prevailing price level, expecting little movement given typical short-term mean-reverting behavior and the absence of any imminent scheduled catalysts. The slight upward tilt in the one-week and one-month estimates reflects a mild positive drift assumption, consistent with longer-run trend behavior seen in many financial assets, but I deliberately kept the drift modest because there was no strong directional signal compelling a more aggressive view in either direction.

Confidence interval widths were calibrated to reflect how uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, realized volatility tends to be relatively contained, so the interval is tight — roughly plus or minus 10 points around the central estimate. By one week, intraweek noise, potential data releases, and sentiment shifts widen the range meaningfully. At one month, the interval expands substantially to reflect the accumulation of daily uncertainties, potential regime changes in market conditions, and macro developments that are difficult to anticipate over that horizon. I also incorporated the well-documented tendency for implied and realized volatility to cluster, meaning calm periods can persist but can also break sharply.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside the stated intervals include unexpected macroeconomic data surprises — such as inflation prints, central bank communications, or employment figures — that force rapid repricing. Geopolitical shocks or sudden liquidity events (flash crashes, forced liquidations) could easily breach even the one-day interval. On the upside, a strongly positive risk-on catalyst, such as an unexpected policy easing signal or a resolution of an ongoing geopolitical tension, could drive prices well above the one-month upper bound of 335.

It is also worth noting that the one-month interval in particular should be treated with humility. Financial distributions have fat tails, meaning extreme outcomes occur more frequently than a simple normal distribution would suggest. My stated 90% confidence intervals are approximations, and the true probability of tail events — say, a move below 250 or above 360 — is non-negligible even if not explicitly reflected in the intervals as stated.
